species.hab: Gardens, parks, meadows, woodland edges. One of Denmark's most familiar butterflies, often hibernates in sheds and attics.
feat: Large eyespots on all four wings — unmistakable
Upperside deep reddish-brown with blue, yellow and black eyespots
Underside almost black, providing camouflage when wings closed
Often basks with wings spread flat on sunny surfaces
Caterpillars black and spiny, gregarious on nettles
species.season: Adults emerge from hibernation March–April. New generation flies July–September before entering hibernation.

conf.d: Red Admiral has red bands rather than eyespots and a very different wing pattern.

species.hab: Gardens, meadows, roadsides, parks. Very common across Sjælland in sunny open habitats.
feat: Orange upperside with black, yellow and blue marginal spots
Row of blue crescents along outer wing edges
Underside dark mottled brown — cryptic when closed
Smaller than Peacock, brighter orange than Comma
Caterpillars black with yellow stripes, on nettles
species.season: Emerges from hibernation March–April. Flies again June–September. Enters hibernation October.

conf.d: Comma has deeply scalloped wing edges and a white 'C' mark on the underside; Tortoiseshell has smoother edges and lacks the C mark.

species.hab: Gardens, orchards, woodland edges. Migratory — arrives from southern Europe each spring, some overwinter in mild years.
feat: Velvety black upperside with striking red-orange bands across forewings
White spots near forewing tips
Hindwing has red-orange border with black spots
Underside mottled brown and blue — beautifully cryptic
Often feeds on rotting fruit in autumn
species.season: Migrants arrive May–June. Most common August–October. Occasionally overwinters in Denmark.

conf.d: Painted Lady is paler orange-pink without the bold red bands; has more diffuse patterning.

species.hab: Open habitats: meadows, farmland, gardens, roadsides. Long-distance migrant from North Africa, numbers vary hugely year to year.
feat: Orange-pink upperside with black markings and white forewing spots
Paler and more muted than Red Admiral
Hindwing underside has row of small eyespots
Strongly migratory — can appear in vast numbers in invasion years
Caterpillars on thistles, mallows, nettles
species.season: Arrives May–June. Peak numbers July–August. Cannot survive Danish winters.

conf.d: Red Admiral is darker with distinct red bands; Painted Lady is paler orange-pink overall.

species.hab: Gardens, allotments, farmland, meadows. Common wherever brassicas are grown.
feat: Upperside white with black forewing tips extending well down the edge
Female has two black spots and a dash on forewing; male has none
Underside yellowish-white
Larger than Small White with more extensive black tips
Caterpillars yellow-green with black spots, gregarious on brassicas
species.season: Two generations: April–June and July–September. Caterpillars a common garden pest.

conf.d: Small White is smaller with less extensive black tips that don't wrap around the forewing edge. Male Small White has one central spot.

species.hab: Gardens, farmland, roadsides, meadows. Extremely common — probably the most frequently seen butterfly in Denmark.
feat: White upperside with greyish (not black) forewing tips
Male has one small central spot on forewing; female has two
Underside of hindwing pale yellowish-green
Smaller and more delicate than Large White
Solitary green caterpillars on brassicas — harder to spot than Large White larvae
species.season: Two to three generations: April–October. Flies on most warm days.

conf.d: Green-veined White has prominent dark scaling along veins on hindwing underside; Small White has uniform pale underside.

species.hab: Damp meadows, woodland rides, hedgerows, gardens. Prefers wilder habitats than other whites.
feat: White upperside similar to Small White
Distinctive grey-green vein markings on hindwing underside — key diagnostic
Veins dusted with dark scales visible at close range
Does NOT feed on brassicas despite the Danish name — caterpillars eat garlic mustard, cuckooflower
Spring generation more heavily marked than summer brood
species.season: Two generations: April–June and July–August. Spring brood more strongly marked.

conf.d: Small White lacks the green-grey vein markings on the hindwing underside; underside is uniform pale yellow.

species.hab: Woodland edges, hedgerows, gardens. Strongly associated with buckthorn (larval food plant).
feat: Male bright sulphur-yellow — unmistakable
Female pale greenish-white, often mistaken for a white butterfly
Uniquely leaf-shaped wings with pointed tips
Small orange spot in centre of each wing
Longest-lived British/Danish butterfly — adults live almost a year
species.season: One of the first butterflies in spring (March). Overwinters as adult in ivy or evergreens. New adults emerge June–July.

conf.d: Female Brimstone can resemble whites but has pointed wing tips and no black markings. Males are distinctly yellow.

species.hab: Woodland edges, hedgerows, gardens. Has expanded range northward in recent decades.
feat: Deeply scalloped, ragged wing edges — unique among Danish butterflies
Upperside rich orange with dark spots
Underside dark brown with a distinctive white comma/C-mark on hindwing
When resting with wings closed, resembles a dead leaf
Caterpillars on hops, nettles, elms
species.season: Overwinters as adult, emerges March. Summer brood July–August. Autumn adults enter hibernation.

conf.d: Tortoiseshell has smooth wing edges and blue marginal crescents; Comma has deeply ragged edges and the white C-mark beneath.

species.hab: Grasslands, meadows, road verges, woodland clearings. One of the most abundant grassland butterflies.
feat: Brown upperside with an orange patch on forewing containing a single black eyespot
Female larger and more orange than male
Male darker brown with smaller orange patch
Underside hindwing mottled grey-brown with variable small spots
Weak fluttering flight low over grass
species.season: Single long-lived generation: flies June–September. Peak in July.

conf.d: Ringlet is darker chocolate-brown without orange patches; has small eyespots with white pupils on underside.

species.hab: Woodland rides, hedgerows, damp meadows, shady lanes. Prefers shadier spots than Meadow Brown.
feat: Uniform dark chocolate-brown upperside
Underside has distinctive small eyespots with white pupils ringed with yellow
Number of eyespots variable — usually 2 on forewing, 5 on hindwing
Flies even in overcast weather when other butterflies rest
Bobbing flight through tall grass and along hedgerows
species.season: Single generation: flies June–August. Peak in July.

conf.d: Meadow Brown has orange forewing patches and a larger single eyespot; Ringlet is uniformly dark with multiple small ringed eyespots.

species.hab: Grasslands, meadows, dunes, road verges, railway banks. Wherever bird's-foot trefoil grows.
feat: Male upperside vivid violet-blue with thin white fringe
Female brown with variable blue dusting at wing bases and orange marginal spots
Underside pale grey-brown with black spots ringed white and orange marginal crescents
Small and fast-flying, often in colonies
Caterpillars on bird's-foot trefoil, attended by ants
species.season: Two generations: May–June and August–September.

conf.d: Small Copper is orange and brown, not blue. Holly Blue (Celastrina argiolus) is paler blue without orange underside spots.

species.hab: Heathland, grassland, road verges, waste ground. Wherever sorrel or dock grows.
feat: Forewing bright coppery-orange with dark spots and brown border
Hindwing dark brown with orange marginal band
Underside forewing orange with spots; hindwing greyish with faint spots
Small, fast, pugnacious — defends territory aggressively
Caterpillars green, slug-shaped, on sorrel and dock
species.season: Two to three generations: April–October. Most common late summer.

conf.d: Common Blue is blue (male) or brown (female), never copper-orange.

species.hab: Flower-rich grassland, meadows, coastal cliffs. Needs bird's-foot trefoil for larvae.
feat: Metallic blue-black forewings with six red spots (3 pairs)
Hindwings bright crimson with narrow dark border
Day-flying moth — often mistaken for a butterfly
Clubbed antennae (slightly thickened at tip)
Produces cyanide compounds — warning coloration is genuine
species.season: Flies June–August. Peak in July. Yellow papery cocoons on grass stems.

conf.d: Five-spot Burnet has five spots (central pair merged) and narrower hindwing border.

species.hab: Gardens, farmland, meadows, everywhere. Migratory — arrives in vast numbers from Mediterranean each year.
feat: Greyish-brown forewings with a distinctive silvery Y or gamma mark
Flies by day and night — often seen hovering at flowers
Fast powerful flight, does not settle long
Long proboscis allows feeding from deep tubular flowers
Numbers vary hugely between years — sometimes in millions
species.season: Migrants arrive May–June. Present until October. Cannot survive Danish winters.

conf.d: Plain Golden Y has a broken or dotted Y-mark rather than a solid silver Y. Much rarer.

species.hab: Gardens, parks, flower-rich borders. Migratory, more frequent in warm summers.
feat: Hovers at flowers exactly like a hummingbird — the most distinctive behaviour
Greyish-brown forewings, orange hindwings visible in flight
Long curved proboscis unfurled while hovering
Produces audible humming from rapid wingbeats
Chunky body with black-and-white tail fan
species.season: Migrants arrive June–September. Occasionally resident in mild winters. Day-flying.

conf.d: Bee Hawk-moth has transparent wing centres and bumblebee-like appearance; Hummingbird HM has opaque wings.

species.hab: Grassland, sand dunes, waste ground, railway banks. Wherever ragwort grows.
feat: Forewings charcoal-black with two red spots and a red streak along leading edge
Hindwings entirely crimson-red
Day-flying, weak fluttering flight
Caterpillars iconic: orange and black striped, gregarious on ragwort
Warning coloration — caterpillars accumulate alkaloids from ragwort
species.season: Adults fly May–July. Caterpillars conspicuous July–September, often defoliating ragwort.

conf.d: Burnet moths have spots not streaks on forewings; burnets are metallic blue-black while Cinnabar is matte black.

species.hab: Gardens, meadows, hedgerows, parks — wherever aphids are found. Denmark's most familiar beetle.
feat: Bright red wing cases (elytra) with exactly seven black spots: 3 on each elytron + 1 shared
Black head with two white patches
Dome-shaped body, round in outline
Produces bitter yellow fluid from leg joints when threatened (reflex bleeding)
Both adults and larvae are voracious aphid predators
species.season: Active April–October. Overwinters communally in leaf litter, bark crevices, buildings.

conf.d: Harlequin is more variable — spot count ranges from 0–21, often larger (6–8 mm), with distinctive M/W mark on pronotum.

species.hab: Old deciduous woodland, parks with veteran oaks. Larvae develop in rotting stumps and roots. Declining across Europe.
feat: Males have enormous antler-like mandibles used in wrestling rivals
Females have smaller but stronger mandibles that can pinch
Chestnut-brown elytra, black head and thorax
Largest beetle in Denmark and northern Europe
Clumsy buzzing flight at dusk in warm June evenings
species.season: Adults active June–August. Males fly at dusk seeking females. Larvae take 3–5 years in rotting wood.

conf.d: Lesser Stag Beetle is entirely black, much smaller (20–32 mm), with only slightly enlarged mandibles.

species.hab: Farmland, gardens, forest edges, parks. Larvae feed on grass and crop roots underground.
feat: Fan-shaped antennae with 7 leaf-like plates (lamellae)
Reddish-brown elytra with fine longitudinal ridges
Pointed abdomen tip extends beyond wing cases
Buzzes loudly when flying — attracted to lights at dusk
White grubs (larvae) are C-shaped, found when digging soil
species.season: Adults swarm May–June (hence 'May bug'). Larvae develop underground for 3 years.

conf.d: Summer chafer is smaller (14–18 mm), flies in June–July, has only 3 antennal lamellae vs cockchafer's 7.

species.hab: Gardens, parks, buildings, farmland. Invasive species from East Asia, now dominant ladybird across Denmark.
feat: Extremely variable colour: orange, red, or black with 0–21 spots
Distinctive M or W-shaped black mark on white pronotum (thorax shield)
Slightly larger and more dome-shaped than native ladybirds
Aggregates in huge numbers on buildings in autumn seeking hibernation sites
Outcompetes native ladybirds and eats their larvae
species.season: Active March–November. Mass aggregations on buildings September–October.

conf.d: Seven-spot always has exactly 7 spots and is pure red; Harlequin is variable. Check the pronotum: Harlequin has M/W mark.

species.hab: Gardens, parks, meadows, forest edges. Larvae in compost heaps and rotting wood.
feat: Brilliant metallic green upperside — iridescent, sometimes with coppery tints
White flecks and irregular lines on elytra
Flies with wing cases closed — side openings allow hindwings to unfurl
Often found inside rose and elderflowers, feeding on pollen
Buzzy, somewhat clumsy flight on warm days
species.season: Adults fly May–September. Larvae in compost heaps year-round.

conf.d: Copper Chafer is more coppery-red with fewer white markings. Less common in Denmark.

species.hab: Everywhere flowers bloom. Managed hives plus feral colonies in tree cavities and buildings.
feat: Golden-brown thorax, banded amber and dark brown abdomen
Dense body hair for pollen collection — hind legs have pollen baskets (corbiculae)
More slender than bumblebees, less hairy
Waggle dance communicates food source locations to nestmates
Barbed stinger — can only sting once, then dies
species.season: Active March–October. Foraging peaks in summer. Colonies overwinter as a cluster.

conf.d: Hoverflies lack pollen baskets, have large eyes, only 2 wings (not 4), and cannot sting. Hoverflies hover motionless; bees don't.

species.hab: Gardens, meadows, parks, farmland. Nests underground in abandoned rodent burrows. Most common bumblebee.
feat: Black body with a single golden-yellow collar band and a buff/off-white tail
Queen very large — one of the biggest Danish bees
Workers smaller with whiter tails than queen
Deep buzzing tone when flying
Short-tongued — sometimes bites holes in flower bases to rob nectar
species.season: Queens emerge February–March. Colonies peak July–August. New queens hibernate from September.

conf.d: Very similar but B. lucorum has a pure white tail (not buff), brighter yellow bands, and a lemon-yellow collar. Reliable ID often requires DNA.

species.hab: Gardens, parks, meadows, walls, rockeries. Nests in stone walls, under paving, sometimes underground.
feat: Jet-black body with a bright red-orange tail — very striking
Males have yellow facial hair and yellow collar band
Dense, velvety fur appearance
Often nests in or under stone structures (hence 'lapidarius' — stone)
Visits a wide range of flowers including lavender, clover, dead-nettles
species.season: Queens emerge March–April. Colonies peak July. New queens from August.

conf.d: Cuckoo bee is a brood parasite of B. lapidarius — very similar but with darker, sparser hair, darker wings, and no pollen baskets.

species.hab: Gardens, meadows, hedgerows, road verges. Builds surface nests in grass tussocks, using moss and grass.
feat: Tawny/ginger-brown thorax, variable brownish abdomen sometimes with darker bands
Smaller and scruffier than other common bumblebees
Long tongue — good at accessing deep flowers like foxglove, honeysuckle
Surface nester — 'cards' (combs) moss and grass to cover nest
One of the last bumblebees still active in autumn
species.season: Queens emerge March–April. Workers into October — one of the longest colony seasons.

conf.d: Moss Carder is more evenly tawny without dark abdominal bands, and much rarer — restricted to coastal and fen habitats.

species.hab: Everywhere: gardens, parks, woodland, buildings. Nests in cavities — underground, in walls, lofts.
feat: Bright yellow and black banded abdomen with an anchor-shaped black mark on face
Narrow waist between thorax and abdomen
Smooth, relatively hairless compared to bees
Carnivorous — hunts insects, scavenges meat, fruit, sugary drinks
Paper nest built from chewed wood pulp
species.season: Queens emerge April. Colonies peak August. Workers most troublesome at picnics late summer when colony breaks down.

conf.d: German Wasp has three black dots on face (not anchor), more extensive black on abdomen, and grey (not tan) nest paper.

species.hab: Old woodland, parks, orchards, rural gardens. Nests in hollow trees, sometimes in buildings.
feat: Much larger than common wasps — queen can reach 35 mm
Chestnut-brown and yellow colouration (not black and yellow)
Reddish-brown thorax and head — distinctly warm-toned
Attracted to lights at night — the only social wasp that flies after dark
Despite fearsome size, less aggressive than common wasps
species.season: Queens emerge May. Colonies peak August–September. Attracted to outdoor lights on warm nights.

conf.d: Common Wasp is much smaller and black-and-yellow (not brown-and-yellow). Hornets have brown on the thorax.

species.hab: Gardens, parks, buildings, woodland. Nests in walls, lofts, underground. Often in proximity to humans.
feat: Yellow and black banded like Common Wasp but face has three black dots (not anchor)
Slightly more extensive black patterning on abdomen
Nest material is grey (mixed wood sources) vs Common Wasp's tan
Equally attracted to sweet foods and protein in late summer
Can be more persistent than Common Wasp at food sources
species.season: Queens emerge April. Peak pest nuisance August–September.

conf.d: Common Wasp has an anchor or dagger mark on face, slightly less black on abdomen, and tan-coloured nest paper.

species.hab: Gardens, meadows, parks, farmland — everywhere. The most common hoverfly in Denmark. Migratory.
feat: Orange-yellow abdomen with distinctive double black bands (thick+thin on each segment)
Hovers motionless in air with superb precision
Only two wings (like all true flies) — hind wings reduced to halteres
Large eyes meeting at top of head (male) or separated (female)
Harmless — no stinger despite bee-like appearance
species.season: Resident plus huge migrant influxes. Flies March–November. Peak summer. Larvae eat aphids.

conf.d: Common Hoverfly has broad solid yellow bands without the distinctive double-band pattern of Marmalade Hoverfly.

species.hab: Gardens, parks, farmland, compost heaps. Common wherever flowers are available.
feat: Excellent honey bee mimic — similar size, colour, and hairy thorax
Dark band across middle of each eye (visible close up)
Single pair of wings (bees have two pairs) — hovers more than bees
Abdomen has variable orange-brown markings
Larvae are 'rat-tailed maggots' found in stagnant water and liquid manure
species.season: Flies March–November. One of the few hoverflies active into late autumn.

conf.d: Honey Bee has 4 wings, pollen baskets on hind legs, longer antennae, and does not hover. Drone Fly has large eyes and only 2 wings.

species.hab: Gardens, meadows, woodland edges, hedgerows. Common and widespread.
feat: Bright yellow abdomen with broad black bands — wasp-like appearance
Bands are solid and evenly spaced (not doubled like Marmalade Hoverfly)
Clear wings, face yellow without a dark central stripe
Females often hover near aphid colonies to lay eggs
Larvae are important aphid predators in gardens
species.season: Flies April–October. Multiple generations. Larvae help control aphids.

conf.d: Marmalade Hoverfly has distinctive doubled black bands (thick+thin). Syrphus has single broad bands per segment.

species.hab: Woodland edges, hedgerows, gardens. Often seen hovering in dappled shade.
feat: Large black hoverfly with a broad white or translucent band across front of abdomen
Translucent whitish panel on abdomen is unique among Danish hoverflies
Darkened wing patches visible in flight
Hovers persistently in shade at woodland edges
Larvae are brood parasites in wasp nests — feed on wasp grubs and debris
species.season: Flies June–September. Most frequent in July near woodland.

conf.d: V. bombylans is furry and mimics bumblebees (orange or white tail forms); V. pellucens is smooth-bodied with a white abdominal band.

species.hab: Ponds, garden pools, lakes, ditches. Often hunts far from water along woodland rides and in gardens.
feat: Large dragonfly — one of the biggest in Denmark
Male: blue spots on black abdomen, green thorax stripes, blue eyes
Female: green spots instead of blue, brown eyes
Patrols a regular beat, often hovering to investigate observers — notably curious
Last two abdominal segments have broad blue/green bands (diagnostic)
species.season: Adults fly July–October. Often the last dragonfly seen in autumn. Larvae aquatic, 2–3 years.

conf.d: Migrant Hawker is smaller with a distinctive yellow triangle (golf-tee shape) at top of abdomen; smaller spots, less blue.

species.hab: Ponds, garden pools, ditches, new water bodies. Often a pioneer at newly dug ponds.
feat: Very broad, flattened abdomen — distinctive shape among Danish dragonflies
Mature male: abdomen powder-blue with yellow side spots
Female/immature: abdomen brown-olive with yellow side spots
Dark basal patches on all four wings
Territorial — perches prominently on waterside vegetation, darting out at rivals
species.season: Adults fly May–August. Often the first dragonfly to colonise new garden ponds.

conf.d: Four-spotted Chaser has a narrower abdomen and four prominent dark spots at wing nodes; lacks the powdery blue colouration.

species.hab: Ponds, lakes, ditches, marshes. The most common dragonfly in Denmark.
feat: Mature male: bright red abdomen — most commonly seen red dragonfly
Female and immature: yellow-brown abdomen
Black legs with a yellow stripe — reliable diagnostic feature
Frequently perches on bare ground, rocks, or posts warming in the sun
Darts out from perch to catch prey, returns to same spot
species.season: Adults fly June–November. One of the last dragonflies of autumn, flying into November in mild years.

conf.d: Ruddy Darter has entirely black legs (no yellow stripe), a more clubbed abdomen, and a more constricted waist.

species.hab: Slow-flowing rivers, streams, canals with muddy bottoms and aquatic vegetation.
feat: Male: metallic blue-green body with a distinctive dark blue band across each wing
Female: metallic green body with pale green-tinted wings
Fluttering, butterfly-like flight — unlike the darting flight of other dragonflies
Rests with wings folded together over body (like a damselfly — it IS a damselfly)
Males perform courtship display flights over water
species.season: Adults fly May–August. Males display and mate along streams and rivers.

conf.d: Male Beautiful Demoiselle has almost entirely dark wings (not banded). Female has browner-tinted wings. Prefers faster, cleaner streams.

species.hab: Ponds, lakes, canals, ditches, garden pools. Common around still or slow-moving water.
feat: Slender, delicate build — typical narrow damselfly shape
Male: sky-blue with black markings including a U-shape on segment 2
Female: green or blue with more extensive black markings
Weak fluttering flight close to water surface and vegetation
Often seen in tandem pairs — male clasps female behind head during egg-laying
species.season: Adults fly May–August. Peak in June. Often the first damselfly to appear at new ponds.

conf.d: Common Blue Damselfly has a 'mushroom' or 'lollipop' mark on segment 2 (not U-shape), and more blue than black on abdomen.

species.hab: Gardens, parks, compost heaps, under bark, in flowers. Omnivorous and nocturnal.
feat: Curved forceps (cerci) at rear — males more curved, females straighter
Reddish-brown body, short leathery forewings
Hidden hindwings fold elaborately to fit under short wing cases (rarely flies)
Nocturnal — hides in dark crevices by day
Females show remarkable maternal care — guard eggs and feed young nymphs
species.season: Active April–October. Females found guarding eggs in soil in spring. Omnivorous year-round.

conf.d: Smaller (7–10 mm), no wing cases visible, more uniformly dark. Much less common.

species.hab: Tall vegetation, hedgerows, woodland edges, garden shrubs. Needs warm sheltered sites.
feat: Very large — one of the biggest insects in Denmark
Bright green with a brown dorsal stripe along wings
Extremely long antennae — much longer than body
Very long hind legs for jumping
Loud, continuous churring song on warm evenings — audible 50 metres away
species.season: Adults July–October. Males sing at dusk and into the night from tall bushes.

conf.d: Grasshoppers are much smaller (15–22 mm), have short antennae, and different song. Bush-crickets have antennae longer than body.

species.hab: Meadows, grassland, road verges, parks. Common in any unmown grass.
feat: Green or brown (variable), compact body with large hind legs
Short antennae — much shorter than body (grasshopper, not cricket)
Vestigial hindwings — cannot fly, only hops
Males produce a brief chirping song by rubbing hind leg against forewing
Song is a brief 1-second buzzing chirp repeated at intervals
species.season: Adults July–October. Song heard from meadows on warm days. Nymphs from May.

conf.d: Field Grasshopper has longer wings that extend beyond abdomen and can fly short distances. Song is a series of 6–10 short chirps.

species.hab: Gardens, hedgerows, woodland edges, window frames. Builds orb webs between structures.
feat: Distinctive white cross pattern on abdomen — formed by pale dots
Colour variable: orange-brown, reddish, or dark brown
Builds large vertical orb webs (up to 40 cm) — classic spider web shape
Sits in centre of web or hides in a retreat to one side, connected by a signal line
Female much larger than male; male risks being eaten during mating
species.season: Most conspicuous August–October when females are large. Eggs overwinter in a silk cocoon.

conf.d: Four-spot has four large white spots in a square pattern instead of a cross. Often redder or greener overall.

species.life: Worker 1–2 years, queen up to 15 years
species.hab: Gardens, pavements, meadows, under stones. The most common ant in Danish gardens.
feat: Uniformly dark brown to black, small size
Workers form long foraging trails to food sources
Tends aphids for honeydew — 'farms' them on plant stems
Winged reproductives emerge en masse on warm humid days ('flying ant day')
Nests under paving stones, in lawns, or in walls — mound of excavated soil visible
species.season: Active March–October. Flying ants swarm July–August, usually after rain followed by warm weather.

conf.d: Yellow Meadow Ant is yellowish-brown, almost entirely subterranean, and builds prominent mounds in old grassland.

species.life: Worker 1–2 years, queen up to 20 years
species.hab: Old grassland, meadows, lawns, pastures. Almost entirely subterranean — rarely seen on the surface.
feat: Yellowish-brown workers — distinctly paler than Black Garden Ant
Builds prominent earth mounds in undisturbed grassland — key field sign
Almost never forages above ground — tends root-feeding aphids underground
Mounds can be very numerous in old pastures, creating characteristic bumpy terrain
Winged reproductives swarm in late summer, often from mound tops
species.season: Active year-round underground. Flying ants swarm August–September. Mounds visible all year.

conf.d: Black Garden Ant is darker brown-black, forages openly on the surface in trails, and does not build prominent earth mounds.

species.hab: Gardens, woodland, hedgerows, meadows, under stones. Prefers damp conditions. Very common across Denmark.
feat: Reddish-brown colour — distinctly reddish compared to Black Garden Ant
Has a functional stinger and will sting if disturbed — noticeable sharp prick
Two-segmented waist (petiole) with a distinct node — visible under magnification
Nests in soil, under stones, in rotting wood, at base of grass tussocks
Aggressively defends nest — workers swarm out and sting when colony is disturbed
species.season: Active March–October. Less conspicuous than Lasius niger — forages more in leaf litter. Swarms August–September.

conf.d: Very similar but has a distinctly stepped antennal scape (bent at base). Difficult to separate in the field without magnification.

species.life: Worker 1–2 years, queen up to 15 years
species.hab: Coniferous and mixed woodland, forest edges. Builds large conspicuous nest mounds from pine needles and twigs.
feat: Large ant — noticeably bigger than garden ants
Reddish-brown thorax and head, dark brown-black abdomen — two-toned appearance
Builds enormous dome-shaped nest mounds up to 1.5 m tall from plant debris
Does not sting but sprays formic acid from abdomen — noticeable vinegar smell
Maintains well-defined trunk trails through forest — some trails persist for years
species.season: Active March–October. Nest mounds visible year-round. Trunk trails busy on warm days.

conf.d: Very similar and often co-occurs. F. polyctena has sparser hair on head and thorax — practically inseparable in the field without microscope.

species.hab: Gardens, hedgerows, woodland, farmland. Adults often enter houses in autumn to hibernate.
feat: Delicate pale green body with large, lacy, transparent wings held tent-like over body
Prominent golden or copper-coloured compound eyes
Long, fine antennae about as long as the body
Slow, weak, fluttering flight — often attracted to lights at night
Larvae are ferocious aphid predators ('aphid lions') — camouflage with debris
species.season: Adults fly May–September. Enters buildings September–October to hibernate (often turns pinkish-brown).

conf.d: C. perla has dark head markings and bluish-green tint; C. carnea is plain pale green with golden eyes. Both are beneficial.

species.hab: Meadows, grassland, hedgerows, gardens, woodland edges. Hunts among low vegetation.
feat: Long-legged brown spider with a pale median stripe running along body
Hunts actively through vegetation rather than building a catching web
Male wraps a fly in silk and presents it to female as a nuptial gift
Female carries egg sac in her jaws, builds a tent-like nursery web for spiderlings
Sunbathes on leaves with front legs stretched forward holding prey
species.season: Adults May–August. Nursery webs visible on bushes June–July. Hunts on warm sunny days.

conf.d: Raft Spider is larger, darker, with white/cream side stripes, and lives on water surfaces. Different habitat.
